 NJVSA holds fundraiser at Waterside in North Bergen dubbed ‘Ghost Signals’
 By Dan Israel - October 31, 2026 1:04 pm 0 
 Share on Facebook 
 Tweet on Twitter 
 The New Jersey Veteran Support Alliance (NJVSA) held their annual fundraising gala at the Waterside Restaurant in North Bergen to support their programs that assist veterans with issues ranging from community events to housing. 
 By Dan Israel/Hudson County View
 The veterans gala drew a crowd of around 100 people, including local politicians such as Hudson County Commissioner Bob Baselice (D-7), who represents North Bergen.
 North Bergen Police Department Sergeant Eric Crafton, an Army National Guard veteran and CEO and President of the NJVSA, joined Director of Marketing Katie Salgado for an interview with HCV at the event.
 “Eric and I started it together, and he started it out of a passion to serve. He was injured himself when he was serving, and got resources to be back. It’s something we talked about for a while, and I do marketing,” noted Salgado.
 Between her and Crafton, she said they were able to make the organization come to life, which now features a swell of volunteers.
 “We do this just because we love it, and it’s a needed service,” Salgado said.
 According to Salgado, this event was their annual fundraiser, which support the various programs that they run.
 “We help navigating the medical system, because it’s complicated. We’ll be a guide sometimes,” she acknowledged.
 NJVSA also helps veterans with housing instability and food insecurity issues.
 “Anytime we get a request for help, we’ll do whatever we can,” Salgado stated.
 Salgado said this was the second year that the organization held their annual fundraiser to support its programs, which she expressed great thanks for.
 “We really appreciate the support of everyone. We couldn’t do this for any of our veterans without everybody’s support, and it’s support in ways sometimes people don’t even realize,” she expressed.
 “Just giving us a like on social media is huge because we have veterans that find us on social media. So anytime we can get the word out, it is helpful. Without the community, we couldn’t do anything.”
 Salgado concluded that the organization normally holds its fundraiser in North Bergen since the township serves as one of NJVSA’s main areas of operations.
 She said it has a significant enough veterans population, as well as Hudson County as a whole, that comes with the need for these resources.
 Following Salgado, Crafton told HCV that NJVSA does tow things, including community events and treatment assistance.
 “We do a lot of community-based events because we’ve noticed that veterans like to isolate themselves,” Crafton said.
 “The other thing that also do is help veterans get the treatment they need and the treatment they need when the VA fails to serve them. We have multiple medical partners that we use for that.”
 According to Crafton, the medical partners with NJVSA usually take insurance, but they also take uninsured veterans he refers to them free of charge.
 He also underscored this was NJVSA’s main fundraising tool, noting that even nonprofits have competitors, albeit in the for-profit sector.
 Crafton, a lifelong North Bergen resident, said that large gatherings of veterans only typically occur at events like this or at American Legions or VFWs.
 “They’re from all different walks of life, and I’ve noticed the younger generation necessarily does not immediately go out and join the VFW,” he asserted.
 “They don’t join the American Legion. So my outreach is a little different. My goal with the events that I do is something that’s family-friendly and fun that they desire to go to that maybe they can’t afford.
 Every year, Crafton said NJVSA takes veterans and their families to American Dream Mall, which donated 3,000 free tickets to Nickelodeon and DreamWorks Water Park for free.
 He said Stranger Things on Broadway also donated over 100 tickets last year to bring out veterans, and they were five rows from the front – tickets that normally sold for $400 each.
 “So the things that we strive to do, it has to be cool, has to be family friendly, and something that they desire, and that’s what typically brings them out,” Crafton explained.
 “Those are the bigger events, but we do have other ones that are more subdued but still fun. I’ll rent out a whole movie theater, for example, and bring veterans out for that.”
 According to Crafton, he also a van he has aptly named “Van Force One” to transport veterans, which they adore and he has since trademarked as he looks to expand the fleet.
 Outside of North Bergen, Hudson County, Bergen County, and Essex County, Crafton said NJVSA has expanded to begin serving Sussex County and Warren County as well.
 In terms of upcoming events, Crafton said that they are again planning for an event at American Dream the weekend prior to Veterans Day.
 In addition, he said NJVSA is organizing giveaways ahead of Christmas and the holiday season.
 “Families that are underserved that don’t have presents for their children, we want to be able to supply that,” Crafton said.
 “That’s where events like this come into play, because as much as I try to pinch every penny that we can from a nonprofit standpoint, there are cases where we have to spend. And that’s where this event is so important.”
 The lavish evening offered an array of free foods, a complimentary cigar, along with other premium cigars for sale, live entertainment – including dancers on stilts and with fire – and the spirit of camaraderie in the name of veterans.
 There were also raffle prizes, a costume contest, and veterans sharing their stories of how NJVSA impacted their lives through programs supported by donations at the fundraiser.
